messages.author: 412aa207a5583264
messages.subject: Question about setting up `hypothesis`
parts:
I'm looking for help interpreting the hypothesis function. Say I have a model with two factors, A and B, and a grouping variable (where only a random intercept is to be estimated for the grouping variable). The first factor has three levels, A1, A2, and A3, whereas factor B has 2: B1 and B2. I set up a model with something like

fit <- brm(y ~ A*B + (1 | group), data=dat)

If I want to look at evidence for the directional hypothesis that A2 is lower than A1 at the level of B1, Is it true that the call is as simple as

hypothesis(fit, "A2 < A1")

Then, if I wanted to look at evidence for the directional hypothesis that A2 is lower than A1 at the level of B2, the call just needs to include the relevant interaction on each side:

hypothesis(fit, "A2 + A2:B2 < A1 + A1:B2")

Second, to what extent does the result of that first hypothesis (however it should be specified) compare to running a separate model with levels A1 and A2 collapsed as a single factor and then comparing the two models with WAIC or LOO? Are there situations with models this simple where it would still be expected that the evidence ratio and WAIC/LOO will give different results?

Thanks,
Patrick

messages.author: 412aa207a5583264
messages.subject: Re: Question about setting up `hypothesis`
parts:
Ah, sometimes airing a question helps with at least part of answering it.

The first hypothesis, is A2 < A1 at B1, should instead be

hypothesis(fit, "A2 < Intercept")

given that in this case (I think?) the effect of A1 at B1 is the Intercept term.

Second, the WAIC/LOO is definitely not the right way to go as an alternative to this hypothesis. Collapsing A2 into A1 disallows an effect of A2 at either B1 or B2, so collapsing isn't a good stand-in for asking about what happens just when B = B1. Is there a different way to construct the formula so as to test this hypothesis through WAIC/LOO model comparison?

messages.author: 6e3dd74b422c061b
messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] Re: Question about setting up `hypothesis`
parts:
The correct way of specifying such hypothesis depends on the coding of the factors. If both A and B are dummy coded (default) with reference category 1, than
A1 vs A2 at B1 should just be "A2 < 0", since the coefficient A2 ist the difference between A2 and the reference (A1) at the reference of all other factors (B1).

The point with LOO and WAIC is actually somewhat different, since you are asking a completely different question, that is "which model provides better out-of-sample predictions?.
Even if you completely collapsed A1 and A2, this might not decrease model fit, since the true difference of A1 and A2 might (for instance) just go into the random intercept if there is no variation of A within each group (i.e. only a certain A level per group).

parts:
Hi Paul,
     Okay, but now I'm worried that I'm misunderstanding something critical because I'm pretty confused by what the marginal_effects plots are showing me in relation to hypothesis. To give a bit more context, I'm doing a bit of exploration with quantile regression, using family = asym_laplace and setting quantile=0.2. In the data I'm working with, the factor A is called "Condition" and can take values of "Not Studied", "CFS", or "Binocular." Factor B is called "cue_correct_fct," and it can take values of "0" or "1". "Not Studied" and "0" are the reference categories, as indicated by

> levels(d$Condition)
[1] "Not Studied" "CFS"         "Binocular"  

> levels(d$cue_correct_fct)
[1] "0" "1"

It seems to be the case that A2 (ConditionCFS) is less than A1 at B1 based on

> hypothesis(fit, "ConditionCFS < 0")
Hypothesis Tests for class b:
                   Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Evid.Ratio Star
(ConditionCFS) < 0    -0.09      0.01     -Inf    -0.06        Inf    *
---
'*': The expected value under the hypothesis lies outside the 95% CI.

So, I thought I would interpret that as evidence for the conclusion that the first quintile in ConditionCFS is lower than the first quintile of the reference Condition (Not Studied) at cue_correct_fct=0.

But when I look at the marginal effects with

> marginal_effects(fit, effects = "Condition:cue_correct_fct")

I don't see how to relate that figure with the results of the hypothesis. I would have thought that either the evidence ratio would be lower in the hypothesis or that there would be a greater distance between the credible intervals of the Not Studied and CFS condition at cue_correct_fct=0. Why isn't that the case?

Thanks for your time,
Patrick

messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] Re: Question about setting up `hypothesis`
parts:
None overlapping CIs (or CIs that don't overlap the estimate of the other group) are just rough proxys of significance, because they don't take correlations between parameters into account.

So, the results of hypothesis and marginal_effects are not opposed to each other. When it comes to testing differences, you need to trust hypothesis.

Say I have a model with two factors, A and B, and a grouping variable (where only a random intercept is to be estimated for the grouping variable). The first factor has three levels, A1, A2, and A3, whereas factor B has 2: B1 and B2. I set up a model with something like

fit <- brm(y ~ A*B + (1 | group), data=dat)

If I want to look at evidence for the directional hypothesis that A2 is lower than A1 at the level of B1, Is it true that the call is as simple as

hypothesis(fit, "A2 < A1")

Then, if I wanted to look at evidence for the directional hypothesis that A2 is lower than A1 at the level of B2, the call just needs to include the relevant interaction on each side:

hypothesis(fit, "A2 + A2:B2 < A1 + A1:B2")

Second, to what extent does the result of that first hypothesis (however it should be specified) compare to running a separate model with levels A1 and A2 collapsed as a single factor and then comparing the two models with WAIC or LOO? Are there situations with models this simple where it would still be expected that the evidence ratio and WAIC/LOO will give different results?

Thanks,
Patrick

Ah, okay. So, is it true that the relevant correlation can be revealed by looking at the dependency between ConditionCFS+Intercept vs. Intercept?

> post <- brms::posterior_samples(fit)
> plot(post$b_ConditionCFS + post$b_Intercept, post$b_Intercept)
> abline(0,1)


 
Although every sample puts ConditionCFS lower than Not Studied at cue_correct_fct=0 (given that the cloud is above the diagonal), the correlation allows the marginals to also overlap.
On Mon, Jan 29, 2018 at 9:15 AM Paul Buerkner <paul.b...@gmail.com> wrote:

None overlapping CIs (or CIs that don't overlap the estimate of the other group) are just rough proxys of significance, because they don't take correlations between parameters into account.

So, the results of hypothesis and marginal_effects are not opposed to each other. When it comes to testing differences, you need to trust hypothesis.
2018-01-29 14:58 GMT+01:00 Patrick Sadil <psa...@gmail.com>:

I expected the marginal_effects plot to provide a graphical preview of the hypothesis, where an overlap between the credible intervals of ConditionCFS and Not Studied at cue_correct_fct=0 would correspond to evidence against the hypothesis that "ConditionCFS < 0". But, hypothesis(fit, "ConditionCFS < 0") returns an evidence ratio of Inf in favor of ConditionCFS having a lower 20th percentile as compared to Not Studied when cue_correct_fct=0. So, it seems like the marginal effects plot and hypothesis are providing different answers to the same question. But, are you saying that's not the case?
On Mon, Jan 29, 2018 at 2:35 AM Paul Buerkner <paul.b...@gmail.com> wrote:
no need to be worried. why would you expect this to be the case?
Patrick Sadil <psa...@gmail.com> schrieb am Mo., 29. Jan. 2018, 01:17:

Hi Paul,
     Okay, but now I'm worried that I'm misunderstanding something critical because I'm pretty confused by what the marginal_effects plots are showing me in relation to hypothesis. To give a bit more context, I'm doing a bit of exploration with quantile regression, using family = asym_laplace and setting quantile=0.2. In the data I'm working with, the factor A is called "Condition" and can take values of "Not Studied", "CFS", or "Binocular." Factor B is called "cue_correct_fct," and it can take values of "0" or "1". "Not Studied" and "0" are the reference categories, as indicated by

> levels(d$Condition)
[1] "Not Studied" "CFS"         "Binocular"  

> levels(d$cue_correct_fct)
[1] "0" "1"

It seems to be the case that A2 (ConditionCFS) is less than A1 at B1 based on

> hypothesis(fit, "ConditionCFS < 0")
Hypothesis Tests for class b:
                   Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Evid.Ratio Star
(ConditionCFS) < 0    -0.09      0.01     -Inf    -0.06        Inf    *
---
'*': The expected value under the hypothesis lies outside the 95% CI.

So, I thought I would interpret that as evidence for the conclusion that the first quintile in ConditionCFS is lower than the first quintile of the reference Condition (Not Studied) at cue_correct_fct=0.

But when I look at the marginal effects with

> marginal_effects(fit, effects = "Condition:cue_correct_fct")

I don't see how to relate that figure with the results of the hypothesis. I would have thought that either the evidence ratio would be lower in the hypothesis or that there would be a greater distance between the credible intervals of the Not Studied and CFS condition at cue_correct_fct=0. Why isn't that the case?

Thanks for your time,
Patrick
On Sun, Jan 28, 2018 at 5:02 PM Paul Buerkner <paul.b...@gmail.com> wrote:

The correct way of specifying such hypothesis depends on the coding of the factors. If both A and B are dummy coded (default) with reference category 1, than
A1 vs A2 at B1 should just be "A2 < 0", since the coefficient A2 ist the difference between A2 and the reference (A1) at the reference of all other factors (B1).

The point with LOO and WAIC is actually somewhat different, since you are asking a completely different question, that is "which model provides better out-of-sample predictions?.
Even if you completely collapsed A1 and A2, this might not decrease model fit, since the true difference of A1 and A2 might (for instance) just go into the random intercept if there is no variation of A within each group (i.e. only a certain A level per group).

2018-01-28 21:02 GMT+01:00 Patrick Sadil <psa...@gmail.com>:
Ah, sometimes airing a question helps with at least part of answering it.

The first hypothesis, is A2 < A1 at B1, should instead be

hypothesis(fit, "A2 < Intercept")

given that in this case (I think?) the effect of A1 at B1 is the Intercept term.

Second, the WAIC/LOO is definitely not the right way to go as an alternative to this hypothesis. Collapsing A2 into A1 disallows an effect of A2 at either B1 or B2, so collapsing isn't a good stand-in for asking about what happens just when B = B1. Is there a different way to construct the formula so as to test this hypothesis through WAIC/LOO model comparison?
